tldr: Instead of detecting failures after contact has already caused damage, this execution monitoring framework looks ahead using a latent world model conditioned on the robot's action plan, predicting failure before contact occurs and safely aborting the motion.
hero_caption: The online monitoring workflow of ContactGuard. Right before the policy initiates gripper closure, a latent world model predicts the future latent state based on the planned action chunk. If the estimated failure probability exceeds a threshold, execution aborts immediately before contact.
overview:
In contact-rich manipulation tasks like grasping, minor misalignments in the gripper often lead to failures such as knocking objects away or slipping. Traditional failure detectors typically react only after physical contact has already occurred. Because such impacts disturb the environment, post-hoc recovery is notoriously difficult.

To address this, the authors asked: can we anticipate whether an upcoming action will fail before the robot ever touches the object? Fortunately, modern visuomotor policies with action chunking output multi-step trajectories in advance, including gripper state changes and approach trajectories. Leveraging this, the authors propose ContactGuard. It feeds the proposed action chunk into a pre-trained latent world model to simulate future states in latent space, then uses a lightweight linear probe on the predicted features to determine grasp success or failure.

Evaluated on a bimanual robot across four real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, ContactGuard achieved AUCs significantly higher than models relying solely on current observations or existing failure detectors. Furthermore, without modifying the underlying manipulation policy, it finishes inference within a brief pre-contact time window (0.5 s), achieving safe pre-contact aborts on hardware without adding control latency.
contributions: Formulated a pre-contact execution monitoring framework for chunked visuomotor policies that predicts future success/failure and aborts right before committing to contact.

Developed ContactGuard, combining an action-conditioned latent world model that quickly predicts multi-view visual embedding dynamics without pixel-level video generation with a lightweight failure probe.

Demonstrated through ablation studies that rolling out planned, specific actions in latent space to obtain future representations is indispensable for accurate failure prediction, compared to relying on current observations or actions alone.
Demonstrated pre-contact aborts on a physical robot without inference lag, requiring neither retraining of the underlying policy nor candidate action sampling/search.

sections.heading: Why wait until impact? Monitoring failures before contact happens
sections.summary: In delicate contact-rich manipulation, minor contact misalignments cause fatal errors, making recovery after disturbing the scene extremely difficult. This work proposes anticipating failure by simulating planned action chunks in a latent world model, aborting execution before contact occurs.
sections.details:
When a robot attempts to grasp an object, subtle errors—such as a gripper slightly off-center, catching an edge, or closing before the object is fully seated—lead directly to failure. Even with wrist cameras, by the time conventional failure detectors trigger, a poor approach has often already disturbed, pushed, or knocked over the object.

Here, the authors leverage the structure of modern imitation learning policies: action chunking. These policies output sequences of consecutive actions that include decisive moments, such as the exact instant of gripper closure. If the robot can anticipate what will happen before completing these actions, it can sense impending failure and stop before physical contact.

While world models naturally fit this lookahead role, heavy and uncertain pixel-level video prediction is unnecessary here. It suffices to preserve the information distinguishing success from failure in a latent space. Following the JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) paradigm—which maps images into compact latent vectors and predicts future representations directly—the authors train an action-conditioned latent world model on unlabelled robot trajectories. This serves as an external, plug-and-play monitor enabling pre-contact aborts without altering the base policy.

captions.F1: Overall system overview. Based on the action chunk generated by the policy, the latent world model predicts the future latent state anchored slightly before contact (gripper closure). If the failure probability exceeds a threshold, execution aborts right before contact.

sections.heading: How it differs from prior work: external verification over candidate search or video generation
sections.summary: This section surveys prior work in latent world models and execution monitoring for robot manipulation. ContactGuard stands out by treating the policy as a black-box proposer and externally verifying a single proposed chunk, rather than co-training models or searching over candidate actions.
sections.details:
To clarify its positioning, the authors distinguish ContactGuard from three related areas:

- Latent world models for manipulation:
Latent world models are widely used in reinforcement learning and model predictive control (MPC), such as Dreamer and TD-MPC, alongside video prediction simulators. ContactGuard builds upon the latent prediction approach of LeWorldModel (LeWM), but repurposes it specifically for pre-contact failure monitoring rather than policy learning or trajectory optimization.

- Failure prediction and execution monitoring:
External success/failure classifiers and out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors (such as FAIL-Detect, RND, and SAFE) have been studied. Methods like SIRIUS co-train the policy and world model in a shared latent space for rollout monitoring. ContactGuard's key distinction lies in its deployment interface: it treats existing policies as black-box proposers without any modifications, allowing an independently trained model to verify pre-planned actions and hold veto power.

- Action chunks and test-time verification:
For policies outputting action chunks (e.g., ACT, Diffusion Policy), some methods sample multiple candidate actions and score them via a world model. In contrast, ContactGuard performs no candidate search; it rapidly evaluates only the single proposed chunk, avoiding search overhead.

sections.heading: Inside ContactGuard: architecture and the pre-contact monitoring mechanism
sections.summary: ContactGuard combines a multi-view latent world model trained on unlabelled data with a linear failure probe trained on a small labelled dataset. Anchoring 0.5 seconds before contact, it predicts the future and makes a safe abort decision just before the gripper closes.
sections.details:
The approach consists of three primary stages:

- 3.1 Problem formulation and data:
Training proceeds in two stages. First, self-supervised learning trains a latent world model on unlabelled robot trajectories using multi-view camera observations and joint-space actions. Next, a lightweight probe is trained on a small set of pre-contact clips with binary success/failure labels to estimate failure probability from predicted future latent features.

- 3.2 & 3.3 Multi-view latent world model:
Images from three cameras are encoded into 192-dimensional embeddings via a shared ViT-Tiny backbone, then aggregated into a single latent state $z_t \in \mathbb{R}^{192}$ through average pooling and a linear projection. This keeps the latent dimensionality constant regardless of camera count while remaining resilient to occlusions. The predictor $P_\theta$ is a 4-layer causal Transformer conditioned via AdaLN-zero using action embeddings. It is trained via teacher-forcing to regress the next latent representation alongside a regularizer (SIGReg) that prevents representation collapse.

- 3.4 Linear probe on predicted latents:
Once the world model is trained, the encoder and predictor are frozen. To capture the post-grasp state, prediction is anchored $k_{\mathrm{pre}}=15$ frames (0.5 s at 30 Hz) before the planned gripper closure time $T_g$. The predictor rolls out autoregressively for $K=30$ steps (reaching 0.5 s past closure). The predicted future latent $\hat{z}_{t+K}$ is normalized and fed into an $L_2$-regularized, class-weighted logistic regression probe to compute the failure probability $P(\mathrm{fail})$.

- 3.5 Online monitoring workflow:
While the policy (ACT) runs, the monitor scans the action chunk to detect the first gripper close command. The moment closure is 15 frames away, the anchor triggers, rolling out the latent state 30 steps ahead and evaluating it with the probe. If $P(\mathrm{fail}) > \tau$, execution aborts immediately before gripper contact. Because inference finishes well within the chunk's execution window, it causes zero control-loop delay.

captions.F2: The internal pipeline of ContactGuard. Multi-view images are aggregated by a ViT encoder into a latent context, and a Transformer rolls out future latent representations conditioned on planned actions. Finally, a frozen logistic regression probe outputs the failure probability.

sections.heading: Real-robot experiments: can it really stop failures before contact?
sections.summary: Evaluated across four contact manipulation tasks on a 14-DoF bimanual robot, multi-view future prediction achieved superior failure prediction accuracy over prior baselines, with inference easily fitting within the pre-contact time budget on an RTX 5090.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on a 14-DoF AgileX Piper bimanual robot equipped with three RGB cameras across four diverse manipulation tasks: cup grasping, box grasping, pencil picking, and towel folding.

- Closed-loop grasp failure prediction (Section 4.2):
Deploying an ACT policy on hardware, when an abort triggered, the robot paused for 5 seconds and then resumed execution to record the counterfactual outcome (50 trials per setting). ContactGuard achieved the highest ROC AUC across all tasks compared to single-view LeWM and external failure detectors (SAFE, FAIL-Detect, RND). On towel folding, where occlusions frequently occur, multi-view aggregation yielded the most pronounced AUC improvement.

- Necessity of future prediction and source of information (Section 4.3):
To address whether future rollouts are truly necessary versus classifying directly from current observations or actions, ContactGuard was compared against a 'Current latent' baseline (using only $z_t$) and a 'Direct baseline' (predicting directly from $(z_t, a)$). ContactGuard using the predicted future latent $\hat{z}_{t+K}$ substantially outperformed both. Furthermore, an action-swap experiment—swapping the planned action with one from another episode while keeping the visual state identical—caused the predicted failure probability to surge (+0.25 on cup, +0.65 on towel). This confirms the model does not merely detect 'visually risky' states, but actively simulates action-dependent failure modes.

- Is proprioception needed?:
Adding the robot's 28-dimensional joint positions and efforts to the input surprisingly degraded test AUC across all four tasks. In limited-data regimes, imperfect multimodal fusion appears to encourage shortcut learning, hindering the model from learning visual contact dynamics.

- Inference latency:
On an NVIDIA RTX 5090, total inference latency—including encoding, 30 rollout steps, and probe scoring—comfortably fit within the 0.5-second pre-contact window, ensuring zero latency impact on the control loop.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: moving beyond aborting failures
sections.summary: ContactGuard demonstrates that pre-contact failures can be prevented with high accuracy without altering the underlying policy. Future challenges include autonomous recovery after an abort and scaling to extended manipulation horizons.
sections.details:
This study shows that action-conditioned latent world models serve not only as tools for planning or representation learning, but also as highly effective pre-contact execution monitors endowed with veto power.

As for limitations, while the framework can predict failure and safely abort motion, it currently lacks an autonomous recovery mechanism to complete the task after stopping. Additionally, the implementation targets a single contact event (gripper closure), focusing on short-horizon contact dynamics contained within the next action chunk.

Future work includes implementing recovery policies that replan from undisturbed, clean post-abort states, as well as integrating with multi-candidate action generators such as Diffusion Policy or Flow Matching to resample and execute alternative safe actions.

sections.heading: Appendix: model implementation details and the limits of direct baselines
sections.summary: Details parameters for ViT-Tiny and the Transformer predictor, alongside comparisons against direct MLP classifiers mapping current states and actions to failure. Even expressive MLPs overfit, reaffirming the value of latent rollouts.
sections.details:
The appendix provides implementation specifics and additional validation results:

- Implementation details (Appendix A):
Input images are resized to $224 \times 224$ and processed by a ViT-Tiny backbone (patch size 16). The architecture uses latent dimension $D=192$, context length $C=3$, training rollout length $L=5$, and test rollout length $K=30$. Models are trained for 100 epochs using AdamW with learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$ and SIGReg weight $\lambda=0.09$.

- Comparison with non-linear direct baselines (Appendix B):
To test whether an MLP mapping $(z_t, a)$ directly to failure without latent rollouts would suffice, the authors swept hyperparameters across hidden layer sizes and dropout rates. Results showed unstable test AUCs that fell far short of ContactGuard. With limited labeled data, learning a direct mapping from $(z_t, a)$ to outcome labels easily overfits. Simulating future states via a self-supervised world model followed by linear classification generalizes far better.

- Task operating points (Appendix C):
Deployment confusion matrices and false-abort rates reveal trade-offs tied to task geometry. Cup grasping showed minimal classification errors, towel folding captured almost all failures at the expense of a slightly higher false-abort rate, and pencil grasping preserved policy success while occasionally missing subtle failures.

takeaways: In contact-rich manipulation, simulating planned action chunks to abort right before contact is far more tractable than attempting post-impact recovery.
Without generating pixel-level video, predicting dynamics in a compact JEPA latent space (~192 dimensions) is sufficient to capture fine geometric interactions determining grasp success.

Direct MLPs predicting outcomes from current observations and actions overfit on small labeled datasets; rolling out futures through a self-supervised latent world model provides crucial inductive bias.
By decoupling the monitor from policy internals to externally verify planned chunks, pre-contact safety mechanisms can be retrofitted onto any existing chunked policy.
limitations: While aborting motions prevents environmental damage, the system currently lacks autonomous recovery capabilities to resume and complete the task post-abort.
The current trigger mechanism relies on a single discrete event (gripper closure); extending to full-horizon tasks requires hierarchical or recurring triggering schemes.
Naively adding robot proprioception (joint positions and efforts) can degrade performance under limited data by inducing shortcut learning that impairs visual interaction modeling.
